title: IFT-BioSim
text:
IFT-BioSim is a farm-level transition modelling framework for examining how agricultural adjustment differs across heterogeneous farms under common national policy objectives.
It asks how opportunity costs, structural conditions, participation decisions, income effects, land reallocation and policy design interact when transition is implemented at farm level.

title: IFT-BioSim
text:
IFT-BioSim is a farm-level transition modelling framework for examining how agricultural adjustment differs across heterogeneous farms under common national policy objectives.
It asks how opportunity costs, structural conditions, participation decisions, income effects, land reallocation and policy design interact when transition is implemented at farm level.

title: IFT-BioSim
IFT-BioSim
text:
Policy instruments
The model can be used to compare alternative instruments and allocation rules, including levies, recycling mechanisms, auction-style approaches and differentiated support.
The purpose is not only to estimate aggregate adjustment, but to understand who responds, who bears costs, and how policy design changes incidence.

title: BioLand-US
text:
BioLand-US asks a practical implementation question:

When a techno-economic model allocates land to perennial biomass, how much of that prospective allocation can also be supported by compatible agricultural land and voluntary contractual participation?

The model does not replace or re-optimise the upstream resource allocation. It adds an explicit implementation layer.

title: BioLand-US
text:

title: BioLand-US
text:
Scientific logic
The framework keeps four quantities distinct:
Techno-economic biomass allocation
        ↓
Compatible agricultural land
        ↓
Contractually accessible land
        ↓
Prospectively mobilised biomass
This makes it possible to distinguish technical allocation from land compatibility and actual access through voluntary contracts.

title: E-SEAT
text:
E-SEAT studies the relationship between fuel-market reform and structural land-use persistence in the U.S. Corn Belt.
Its central question is:

If the ethanol-demand signal weakens, how much of current Corn Belt specialisation is likely to reverse, and how much reflects the production structure already in place?

title: E-SEAT
text:
E-SEAT studies the relationship between fuel-market reform and structural land-use persistence in the U.S. Corn Belt.
Its central question is:

If the ethanol-demand signal weakens, how much of current Corn Belt specialisation is likely to reverse, and how much reflects the production structure already in place?

title: E-SEAT
text:
Design
The framework links county-level agricultural data, national corn-ethanol demand, predetermined county conditions, fixed-effects estimation, dynamic analysis, scenario translation, backcasting and spatial diagnostics.
The empirical structure covers counties across the Corn Belt over repeated Census of Agriculture waves from 1997 to 2022.

title: E-SEAT
text:
Main distinction
The analysis separates responsiveness from starting position.
A county may respond to a weaker ethanol-demand signal and still remain highly specialised because it begins from a very different agricultural structure.

title: Research
text:
My research focuses on ex-ante modelling of agricultural, land-use, bioenergy and environmental policy. I am interested in what happens between a policy target and its eventual implementation: how technical assumptions translate into changes in production, land use and behaviour, how those changes are distributed across places and producers, and what that means for policy design.
A central theme is that national objectives are implemented through heterogeneous production systems, land resources, farms and places. Aggregate feasibility therefore does not guarantee local feasibility, economic accessibility or behavioural participation.

title: Research
text:
Research questions
Much of my work follows a common sequence:
Policy objective or proposed intervention
        ↓
Technical and economic assumptions
        ↓
Production-system response
        ↓
Spatial and regional incidence
        ↓
Economic and behavioural response
        ↓
Opportunities, constraints and uncertainty
        ↓
Policy design, targeting and implementation
Questions include:

How can national agricultural, land-use and bioenergy objectives be translated into realistic spatial and economic pathways?
Where do transition costs, opportunities and implementation constraints concentrate?
Which technically available resources remain economically accessible and realistically deployable?
How do alternative incentives, compensation rules and allocation principles change who bears adjustment?
How can national pathway models be connected to local geography and farm-level heterogeneity?
What can be learned before major policy and investment decisions become difficult to reverse?

title: Research
text:
Agricultural and land-use transitions
This work examines AFOLU mitigation, livestock restructuring, afforestation, wetland rehabilitation, anaerobic digestion, bioeconomy pathways, land-use competition and long-term transition planning.
Rather than treating land release and land opportunity as equivalent, the modelling separates transition-space release, physical resource, eligibility, opportunity, allocation and actual adoption.

title: Research
text:
Spatial and distributional modelling
I use spatial reconstruction, local-area allocation, microsimulation and synthetic populations to investigate how nationally coherent changes are distributed across geography.
This includes transition exposure, land capability, released-land opportunity, regional heterogeneity and place-sensitive policy analysis.

title: Research
text:
Behavioural and policy-response modelling
A second strand examines producer response to policy instruments, including participation, stocking-rate adjustment, opportunity costs, compensation design, additionality and heterogeneous responses to alternative incentives.
The aim is to distinguish technical potential from economic accessibility and actual willingness to participate.

title: Research
text:
Bioenergy and resource mobilisation
My bioenergy work examines how resource estimates change when land competition, economic opportunity costs, contractual access and heterogeneous participation are introduced.
This includes Irish biomethane and land-use pathways as well as U.S. biomass, biofuel and land-access applications.

title: Research
text:
Food, climate and development
I also maintain a broader interest in food-system sustainability, agricultural productivity, carbon pricing, sustainable diets and climate-development trade-offs, including questions relevant to Sub-Saharan African food systems.

title: Research
Research
text:
Reusable modelling systems
The longer-term objective is to build reusable modelling and decision-support systems, not just one-off analyses. Where possible, projects are structured so that assumptions, data requirements, scenario controls, code, tests and outputs can be inspected and extended by other researchers and analysts.

title: Why I’m Excited to Work with FUSION and FORESIGHT
text:
FORESIGHT project illustration. Source: FUSION, University of Galway.


One of the most exciting parts of my PhD journey has been working in the FUSION research environment at the University of Galway and contributing to research connected with FORESIGHT.
FUSION stands for FUture Sustainable economy Integrated mOdelling Network. What attracts me to the group is that it does not treat sustainability as a problem that belongs to one discipline. Its work brings together life-cycle assessment, integrated assessment modelling, land-use analysis and environmental software engineering. The common thread is the use of quantitative models to ask practical questions about how economies, food systems and landscapes could change in the future.
That way of thinking fits naturally with the questions that interest me.
Agriculture and land use are full of difficult trade-offs. A national climate target can look clear on paper, but implementation happens through real production systems, farms, forests and communities. A pathway that appears technically feasible at national scale may look very different once land availability, livestock systems, economic incentives, spatial variation and alternative uses of land are considered.
This is where FORESIGHT, or Future ORiEnted ScenarIo modellinG of Holistic land use sTrategies, becomes especially interesting. The project provides agriculture and land-use modelling evidence for Ireland and continues the development of integrated AFOLU modelling tools such as GOBLIN. Its emphasis is not simply on predicting one future. It is about exploring plausible pathways, testing assumptions and understanding what different choices could mean for emissions, land use, resilience and wider sustainability objectives.
For me, that distinction matters. Forecasting asks what is likely to happen. Foresight asks a broader question: what futures are possible, what would be required to reach them, and what might we learn by working backwards from those outcomes?
My own work increasingly sits in that space. I am interested in taking national agricultural and land-use pathways and resolving them into more detailed spatial and farm-level questions. Where does adjustment occur? Which production systems are most exposed? What alternatives are actually feasible in particular places? How do economic and behavioural responses change the picture? And how can models become reusable decision-support tools rather than one-off academic exercises?
Working alongside researchers developing GOBLIN and related modelling approaches has reinforced something I increasingly value in research: the model itself is not the final product. The useful output is better evidence for a difficult decision.
That is what makes FUSION and FORESIGHT exciting to me. They create a space where environmental science, economics, modelling and software can meet around real policy problems, while keeping the analytical work transparent and open to improvement.
I expect many posts on this site will grow from that environment. Some will explain models and methods. Others will discuss new papers, data, land-use questions, agriculture, bioenergy or interesting developments in Ireland, the United States and elsewhere.
The aim is simple: use the blog as a place to think in public, connect research to current questions, and make technical work easier to understand.

title: About
text:
I am a PhD Researcher and Research Assistant in Plant & AgriBiosciences at the University of Galway’s Ryan Institute.
My research sits at the intersection of agricultural economics, land-use modelling, environmental policy and quantitative decision support. I am particularly interested in the gap between a national target and what implementation actually means for different farms, production systems, land resources and places.

title: About
text:
Research
My work spans agricultural and livestock transitions, land-use change, spatial feasibility, economic exposure, heterogeneous policy response, bioenergy opportunities, and policy design and implementation.
Rather than treating every question at one scale, I use the resolution that fits the decision. Some problems need national pathways, others local geography, and others farm-level or individual-operation detail.
Current modelling work includes GOBLIN-Spatial, AGRISYN, IFT-BioSim, BioLand-US and E-SEAT.

title: About
text:
Methods
I work across econometrics, spatial modelling, synthetic populations, microsimulation, optimisation, scenario analysis and reproducible computational workflows, using tools including Python, R, Stata, GIS and SQL.

title: About
text:
Reproducible research
I use GitHub to organise analytical workflows, document assumptions and make models easier to inspect and reproduce. My longer-term aim is to build reusable modelling and decision-support infrastructure rather than a collection of one-off analyses.
Where source data are confidential or restricted, public repositories can still provide code, assumptions, data-access notes, scenario controls, validation checks and instructions for authorised reproduction.

title: About
text:
Background
I hold an MSc in Management Science and Engineering, completed in China, and currently undertake doctoral research at the University of Galway.
My academic work has developed across management science, agricultural and environmental economics, econometrics, sustainability policy and computational modelling.
